_comment: Secure-by-design pattern catalog (CONTRACTS §5). whyTemplate uses {appName}. 'when' selects the pattern from the design profile; for patterns, 'external-apis' means any outbound connection (external APIs, the AI provider or a mail server) — see patternApplies() in server/src/frameworks/applicability.ts.

patterns.name: Separate trust zones
patterns.description: The app is split into zones that trust each other as little as possible: the browser (never trusted), the app (trusted, listens only on this computer by default), the data (database and files protected by file permissions) and outside providers (reached only through an allow-list). Everything crossing a boundary is checked.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} keeps web pages, its own logic, its data and outside services in separate compartments, so a problem in one cannot spread to the others.

patterns.name: Deny by default
patterns.description: Every page and API route must state who may use it before it exists. A route with no declared access rule is refused at start-up, so nothing can be reachable by accident.
patterns.whyTemplate: Because {appName} has sign-in, every page must say who is allowed to open it; anything not explicitly allowed is refused.

patterns.name: Least-privilege roles
patterns.description: Each role gets only the access it needs. Records that belong to a person can be opened only by that person or an administrator, and the rules are documented automatically from the code.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} has different kinds of users, so each role only sees and changes what its job requires, and people can only open their own records.

patterns.name: Secure browser defaults
patterns.description: Every response tells the browser to behave safely: only run scripts the app itself provides, never show the app inside another site, never guess file types, and keep the sign-in cookie out of reach of scripts.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} sends browser protection headers on every page, which blocks whole families of attacks such as injected scripts and click-jacking.

patterns.name: Contract-first input rules
patterns.description: Every route declares exactly which fields it accepts and what they must look like. Unknown fields and wrong types are rejected, and the API description (openapi.json) is generated from the same declarations.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} checks every piece of input against a strict description before using it, so malformed or unexpected data is refused at the door.

patterns.name: Fail securely
patterns.description: When something goes wrong the app stops safely: people see a short generic message, details go to the log only, and a failed check always means 'no' rather than 'let it through'.
patterns.whyTemplate: If something breaks inside {appName}, it fails closed and never shows internal details that could help an attacker.

patterns.name: Security events are logged
patterns.description: Sign-ins, refused access, rejected input, rate-limit hits, administrator actions and unexpected errors are written as structured log lines with a request id, and sensitive values are redacted.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} records who did what and when, so you can investigate a problem later without exposing passwords or personal data in the logs.

patterns.name: Tamper-evident audit log
patterns.description: Security events also go into an append-only audit table where each entry is chained to the previous one with a hash. A command verifies the chain, and entries are kept for at least a year.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} keeps an audit trail that shows if anyone tried to alter or delete past records of what happened.

patterns.name: Safe to repeat
patterns.description: Requests that change data can be repeated safely: an Idempotency-Key header returns the stored answer instead of acting twice, unique constraints stop duplicate records, and edits check that nobody else changed the record in between.
patterns.whyTemplate: If a request to {appName} is sent twice by mistake (a double click or a flaky connection), nothing is created or charged twice.

patterns.name: Timeouts and health checks
patterns.description: Every incoming request and every outbound call has a time limit, the app shuts down cleanly, and /healthz and /readyz let a monitoring tool check that it is alive without revealing anything else.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} never hangs waiting forever, and a monitoring tool can check that it is up.

patterns.name: Rate limits and quotas
patterns.description: Sign-in, registration, password reset, the assistant, uploads and all other routes have request limits, with increasing delays and a temporary lock on repeated failed sign-ins. Each person has a quota for what they can create.
patterns.whyTemplate: Nobody can guess passwords by trying thousands of times or flood {appName} with requests.

patterns.name: Secrets outside the code
patterns.description: Keys and passwords live only in a protected .env file that SecureVibe fills with strong random values. The app refuses to start with weak or placeholder secrets, and secrets never appear in code, logs or reports.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName}'s secret keys are generated for you, kept out of the code and checked at start-up, so a leaked copy of the code does not leak the keys.

patterns.name: Data classification
patterns.description: Every kind of information the app stores is listed with a protection level and an owner. Fields marked sensitive are encrypted, redacted in logs and never placed in web addresses.
patterns.whyTemplate: Because {appName} stores information about people, every kind of data is listed with how it is protected and who is responsible for it.

patterns.name: Sensitive fields encrypted
patterns.description: Fields marked sensitive are encrypted inside the database with AES-256-GCM. Keys are versioned and can be rotated with a command, and the cryptography in use is documented automatically.
patterns.whyTemplate: Because {appName} handles sensitive information, those fields are encrypted where they are stored, so a copied database file does not reveal them.

patterns.name: Keep only what is needed
patterns.description: A written retention rule says how long each kind of information is kept. People can export or delete their own data, administrators can delete accounts, and when a retention period is set a background job removes or pseudonymises old records.
patterns.whyTemplate: Because {appName} stores information about people, there is a clear rule for how long it is kept and a way to delete it.

patterns.name: Two-factor authentication for administrators
patterns.description: Administrators must add a second sign-in step with an authenticator app (time-based codes). Recovery codes are hashed and single-use, code entry is rate limited, and losing the second factor requires an administrator to reset it with a logged reason.
patterns.whyTemplate: Administrators of {appName} can do the most damage if their password leaks, so they must also enter a code from an authenticator app.

patterns.name: Two-factor authentication for everyone
patterns.description: Every user can turn on a second sign-in step with an authenticator app from their account page. Turning it off requires re-entering the password.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} needs a higher level of protection, so every user can add a second sign-in step, not only administrators.

patterns.name: Outbound connections on an allow-list
patterns.description: The app can only connect to the outside addresses listed in its settings. All outbound calls go through one client with timeouts, a response size cap, certificate checks, no automatic redirects and a circuit breaker. This also applies when the only outside services are the AI provider or a mail server.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} talks to outside services, so it may only reach the addresses on its allow-list and never follows a link somewhere unexpected.

patterns.name: Uploads kept at arm's length
patterns.description: Uploaded files are size-capped while streaming, checked by their real content (not just the file name), limited to safe types, renamed to random names, stored outside the web folder and handed back as downloads only, with an ownership check and a per-user quota.
patterns.whyTemplate: Because people can upload files to {appName}, every file is checked, renamed and stored where it can never run as a web page.

patterns.name: AI assistant guard-rails
patterns.description: Text sent to the assistant is cleaned, length-limited and screened for prompt-injection attempts; the assistant only sees data the signed-in person may see; its answers are checked against a fixed format and length, filtered for leaked instructions, and shown as plain text. Every call is logged with token counts, per-user budgets apply, and an administrator can switch the assistant off instantly.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} includes an AI assistant, so everything going in and coming out of it is checked, budgeted and logged, and you can switch it off at any time.

patterns.name: A person approves AI actions
patterns.description: The assistant can only use a fixed list of tools with strict input and output rules. Any tool that changes data returns a proposal that the person must confirm on screen before the app carries it out under that person's own permissions. The model never executes anything itself.
patterns.whyTemplate: The assistant in {appName} may change records, so every change is shown to the person first and only happens after they confirm it.

patterns.name: Locked and listed dependencies
patterns.description: The exact versions of every third-party package are locked in a tested lockfile that the generator cannot change; install scripts are disabled; a software bill of materials is produced and the documentation states how quickly vulnerable packages must be updated.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} uses a fixed, tested set of third-party packages, with a list of what is inside and a rule for how fast to update when a problem is found.

patterns.name: Incident response plan
patterns.description: A written plan says who to contact, what to do first, how to preserve evidence and how to communicate if something goes wrong, together with a security contact and a deployment guide.
patterns.whyTemplate: If something goes wrong with {appName}, you have a short written plan to follow instead of improvising.

patterns.name: HTTPS in front of the app
patterns.description: When the app is reached over a network it runs behind an HTTPS reverse proxy (or with its own certificate on a local network). The app then sends HSTS, marks cookies Secure with the __Host- prefix and only trusts the client address reported by the configured proxy.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} is meant to go online later, so it is prepared to run behind HTTPS and the deployment guide makes that the first step.

patterns.name: API keys for other programs
patterns.description: Other programs connect with a random API key that is stored hashed, sent only in the Authorization header (never in the web address), limited to API routes, rate limited per key, and can be revoked at any time.
patterns.whyTemplate: Other programs can connect to {appName}, so each one gets its own key that can be limited and revoked without affecting anyone else.

patterns.name: Payments handled by a provider
patterns.description: Card details never touch the app. Payments go through a payment provider's own hosted checkout page, and the app only stores the provider's reference for each payment. A setup guide explains how to connect a provider.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} takes payments, so card numbers are handled entirely by a payment provider and never stored in your app, which keeps you out of the strictest card-industry rules.

patterns.name: Background jobs under control
patterns.description: Scheduled jobs are declared in code, never built from user input, recorded in a jobs table with a lock so the same job cannot run twice at once, and written so that re-running one is safe.
patterns.whyTemplate: {appName} runs tasks in the background, so each task is locked while it runs and safe to repeat if the app restarts.
